blocks.text: Working with databases in Python means storing and managing data in a database system. Python programs can connect to databases to insert, retrieve, update and delete data. Databases let applications handle large amounts of information efficiently and keep data accurate and consistent. Python supports database work through built-in and external libraries.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Databases let programs store large amounts of information safely and retrieve it quickly when needed.

blocks.title: Database
blocks.text: A database is an organised collection of data stored in a structured format, so that the data can be accessed and managed easily.
Databases reduce duplicated data, improve reliability and support secure storage, and they are used in many kinds of software.

blocks.caption: Basic database ideas
rows: Entity
A real-world object, person, place, event or concept about which data is stored
Student, Teacher, Course, Book, Employee
Attribute
A property or characteristic of an entity
For Student: name, roll number, class, age
Relationship
How two or more entities are connected
A Student enrols in a Course
Identifier
An attribute that uniquely identifies each record of an entity
Roll number, because each student's is unique

items: Relational database: stores data in tables of rows and columns and links the tables through relationships.
Table: a collection of related data organised in rows (records) and columns (fields).
Column: a property of an entity, such as name or age.
Primary key: a unique identifier for each record in a table.
Foreign key: a field that links one table to another by referring to the other table's primary key.

Row 102 is outlined as a record and the Name column as a column (attribute). An arrow labelled DeptID refers to Department.DeptID runs to table Department, whose primary key DeptID has rows 1 Computer Science, 2 Electronics and 3 Mechanical.

blocks.text: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to work with relational databases; its commands create, read, update and delete data.

A connection to the database is needed before any data operation. The sqlite3 library is built into Python and suits small databases: it keeps the whole database in a single file. MySQL is used for larger, more complex systems; its connection needs details such as the database name and credentials. Once connected, Python can add, retrieve and modify data, and the connection should be closed properly afterwards.

blocks.title: Example: create a table, insert and read with sqlite3 (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import sqlite3

# Connect to school.db (created automatically if missing)
connection = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cursor = connection.cursor()     # runs SQL queries

cursor.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students
....(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, age INTEGER, grade TEXT)""")

# (Optional) insert sample data
cursor.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, age, grade) VALUES ('Ali', 14, '8th')")
cursor.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, age, grade) VALUES ('Sara', 15, '9th')")
connection.commit()               # save changes

cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM students")
records = cursor.fetchall()       # list of rows
for row in records:
....print(row)

connection.close()

items: Connect to the database: sqlite3.connect() opens the school.db SQLite database.
Create a cursor: the cursor object runs SQL commands.
Execute a query: cursor.execute() runs the SQL query that fetches all records from the students table.
Fetch and display: fetchall() returns all the rows, which are printed one by one.

blocks.text: CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update and Delete, the basic actions on stored data (Fig 4.4 and Table 4.1). Every database application depends on them to keep information accurate and up to date, and Python performs them by sending SQL commands through a cursor.

blocks.caption: Table 4.1 CRUD operations
rows: Create
INSERT INTO students (ID, Name, Age) VALUES (1, 'John', 20);
Adds a new record to a table
Read
SELECT * FROM students;
Retrieves data from a table; the data is not changed
Update
UPDATE students SET Age = 21 WHERE ID = 1;
Modifies an existing record; only the rows matching the condition change
Delete
DELETE FROM students WHERE ID = 1;
Removes a record; the condition limits which rows are removed

blocks.alt: A small students table (ID, Name, Age: 1 Ibrahim 25, 2 Zainab 30, 3 Kiran 28) in the middle with four arrows pointing to it: Create (INSERT ...) and Read (SELECT ...) at the top, Update (UPDATE ...) and Delete (DELETE ...) at the bottom. A note says Read does not change the data, while Create, Update and Delete do and need commit().
blocks.caption: The four CRUD operations on a table (original diagram after Fig 4.4).
blocks.long_description: Three of the four operations change the table; that is why Python must call commit() after them.

items: Create (adding new records): SQL INSERT commands store new data, which becomes part of the table once executed.
Read (retrieving and displaying data): SQL SELECT commands fetch stored records; Python processes the results.
Update (modifying existing records): SQL UPDATE commands change selected records when stored information needs correction; only the specified data changes.
Delete (removing data safely): SQL DELETE commands with conditions remove only the selected records; careful use prevents losing important data.

blocks.text: Update a student's marks and display the updated data.

blocks.title: Example: deleting a record (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cursor = connection.cursor()

# Delete the student with ID = 1
cursor.execute("DELETE FROM students WHERE ID = 1")
connection.commit()               # without commit() the delete is not permanent
print("Record deleted successfully")

connection.close()
